cards.front:
Video analysis:
from video to physical quantities?
cards.back:
From image sequences,
position data $s(t)$ are determined.

From this and the time intervals between frames, $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ follow.

$v_{n+1}=v_n+a_n\,\Delta t$,
$s_{n+1}=s_n+v_n\,\Delta t$

with time step $\Delta t$,
$a_n=a(t_n, s_n, v_n)$,
$t_{n+1}=t_n+\Delta t$.

cards.front: Sports physics: most important influencing factors?
cards.back: Initial speed, launch angle, force application, friction, and air resistance determine the motion process

cards.back:

Area under $t$-$a$ is $\Delta v$

$v(t)=gt$

cards.back:

the velocity vector remains constant

Same magnitude,

cards.back: $E_\text{tot}= \text{constant}$

In closed systems, total momentum remains conserved:

$\sum \vec p= \text{constant}$

if $\sum \vec F_\text{ext}=0$, then $\sum \vec p$ is constant
$\vec J= \int \vec F\,dt \approx \vec F\,\Delta t= \Delta \vec p$

Total momentum remains conserved

kinetic energy is not conserved

reduces average force:

Total momentum and total kinetic energy remain conserved

cards.back: Energy is conserved, but its usability decreases due to entropy production

cards.front: Rotational energy and moment of inertia?
cards.back:
$E_\text{rot}= \frac12 I \omega^2$

$I$ depends on mass distribution relative to the rotation axis
An external torque changes the direction of angular momentum and causes precession

For nearly constant angular momentum, a smaller

moment of inertia $I$

leads to larger angular speed $\omega$

cards.front: Figure skating: Why does a skater spin faster when pulling in their arms?
cards.back:
Without external torque, angular momentum is conserved: $L = I\omega = \text{constant}$


When pulling the arms in, $I$ decreases, so $\omega$ increases. The skater performs muscular work; this increases rotational energy $E_\text{rot}= \frac12 I \omega^2$

Mnemonic: When pulling the arms in, angular momentum remains conserved, rotational energy increases.
